**1. Calculate the energy provided by the voltage:**
The energy $E$ supplied to an electron by a potential difference $V$ is given by $E = eV$. For a mole of electrons, the energy is $E_{mol} = F \times V$, where $F$ is the Faraday constant.
From the constants page (G0-3), $F = 96,485 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$.
Given $V = 2.5 \text{ V}$ (which is $2.5 \text{ J C}^{-1}$):
$$E_{mol} = 96,485 \text{ C mol}^{-1} \times 2.5 \text{ J C}^{-1} = 241,212.5 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx 241 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Alternatively, using electronvolts:
$1 \text{ eV} \approx 96.485 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
$2.5 \text{ eV} \approx 2.5 \times 96.485 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \approx 241.2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

**2. Compare with Bond Dissociation Energies (BDE):**
For the dehalogenation (bond breaking) to occur via this mechanism, the energy supplied by the electrons must be greater than or equal to the bond dissociation energy of the C-X bond.
$$E_{supplied} \ge \text{BDE}(\text{C-X})$$
$$241 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \ge \text{BDE}(\text{C-X})$$

Looking at the provided table:
*   **C-F:** $467 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ ($467 > 241$, bond will not break)
*   **C-Cl:** $346 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ ($346 > 241$, bond will not break)
*   **C-Br:** $290 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ ($290 > 241$, bond will not break)
*   **C-I:** $228 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ ($228 < 241$, bond can break)

Only the Carbon-Iodine bond has a dissociation energy low enough to be broken by electrons with 2.5 eV of energy.

**Conclusion:**
The halogen must be Iodine (I).

X = I

    *   **Cycle $k$:**
        *   $R_k = F(1-\eta) + F(1-\eta)^2 + \dots + F(1-\eta)^k$.
        *   This is a geometric series sum: $R_k = F(1-\eta) \frac{1 - (1-\eta)^k}{1 - (1-\eta)} = F \frac{1-\eta}{\eta} (1 - (1-\eta)^k)$.
